t: Runtime Security Analysis of Monolithic 3D Embedded DRAM with Oxide-Channel Transistor
pb: Monolithic 3D eDRAM with oxide-channel transistors is vulnerable to Rowhammer/Rowpress attacks and M3D-specific electrical disturbances that degrade data integrity and security.
me: Characterizes Rowhammer/Rowpress vulnerabilities in IWO eDRAM across 2D and M3D configurations; examines electrical disturbances from memory-on-logic and memory-on-memory stacking; evaluates physical design and architecture mitigation strategies.
nv: First comprehensive security and disturbance analysis of M3D eDRAM with oxide-channel transistors identifying M3D-specific vulnerability vectors.
th: Security of 3D embedded DRAM with oxide transistors

t: One More Motivation to Use Evaluation Tools This Time for Hardware Multiplicative Masking of AES
pb: Prior hardware implementations of multiplicative masking for AES contain critical vulnerabilities in the Kronecker delta function that leak information under side-channel analysis.
me: Evaluates prior multiplicative masking design (De Meyer et al. CHES 2018) using PROLEAD evaluation tool under glitch-and-transition-extended probing model; identifies leakage in first-order Kronecker delta; proposes improved randomness optimization.
nv: Identifies critical vulnerability in prior SOTA multiplicative masking design and demonstrates effective fix via improved randomness optimization.
th: Side-channel secure multiplicative masking for AES

t: Hardware/Software Runtime for GPSA Protection in RISC-V Embedded Cores
pb: Existing hardware countermeasures against fault attacks require compiler modifications and cannot protect indirect jumps; protecting unmodified binaries is not supported.
me: Hardware/software runtime generates Generalized Path Signature Analysis (GPSA) signatures during execution of unmodified off-the-shelf RISC-V binaries; signatures validate control-flow and code integrity through continuous monitoring.
nv: First solution providing fault attack protection on unmodified RISC-V binaries without compiler modifications, supporting indirect jumps.
th: Runtime fault attack protection for RISC-V

t: SAFELOC: Overcoming Data Poisoning Attacks in Heterogeneous Federated Machine Learning for Indoor Localization
pb: Indoor localization systems suffer from device heterogeneity (hardware/software variations across mobile devices) and ML data poisoning attacks, compromising both accuracy and model efficiency for deployment.
me: SAFELOC combines a fused neural network performing concurrent poisoning detection and localization with federated learning, employing a dynamic saliency map-based aggregation strategy that adapts based on detected poisoning severity.
nv: Dynamic saliency-map-driven federated aggregation that adapts poisoning defense to attack severity while maintaining model compactness.

mx.speedup: 5.9× mean error, 7.8× worst-case, 2.1× latency

th: federated learning for robust heterogeneous mobile localization

t: Protecting Cyber-Physical Systems via Vendor-Constrained Security Auditing with Reinforcement Learning
pb: CPS security requires vendor diversity for mutual auditing against hardware Trojans, but multi-vendor integration creates cost and maintenance challenges with insufficient vendor availability.
me: Vendor-constrained security auditing framework combines side auditing (detects HT collusion) with infected node isolation; multi-agent cooperative reinforcement learning optimizes device-to-vendor assignment minimizing offline nodes.
nv: Multi-agent cooperative RL solves device-to-vendor assignment for hardware-Trojan-resilient CPS with minimal vendor diversity.

mx.other: 40.95% vendor reduction, 0.39% infected node increment

th: RL-based CPS security auditing with vendor constraints

t: Compromising the Intelligence of Modern DNNs: On the Effectiveness of Targeted RowPress
pb: RowPress attacks can flip targeted bits in DRAM similar to RowHammer; impact on deep neural networks unexplored. Existing RowHammer mitigation mechanisms are ineffective against RowPress, creating a new DNN vulnerability.
me: DRAM-profile-aware attack methodology capturing distinct bit-flip patterns of RowPress versus RowHammer. Comparative evaluation across eleven DNN architectures and multiple benchmark datasets on Samsung DRAM chips.
nv: First comprehensive evaluation of RowPress attacks on DNNs and comparison demonstrating faster degradation than RowHammer.

mx.other: RowPress causes faster performance degradation than RowHammer

th: RowPress DRAM attack vulnerability in deep neural networks

t: Azure Secure Hardware Architecture : A Robust Security Foundation for Cloud Workloads
pb: Cloud infrastructure requires hardware-level security primitives to protect workloads from unauthorized access and side-channel attacks in multi-tenant environments.
me: Azure's architecture integrates cryptographic attestation, secure execution contexts, and hardware-managed key isolation within CPU microarchitecture. It extends trusted execution environments (TEEs) with cloud-specific threat models and integrates security properties into processor design.
nv: Unified security architecture combining CPU, firmware, and hypervisor to provide cryptographic proof of hardware and software integrity for cloud tenants.
th: Hardware-backed cloud security attestation

t: Efficient Memory Side-Channel Protection for Embedding Generation in Machine Learning
pb: Embedding table lookups in ML models (DLRMs, LLMs) leak sensitive input features (user IDs, token indices) through memory access patterns, making them vulnerable to side-channel attacks; protecting these accesses with conventional ORAM incurs prohibitive overhead due to the massive size of embedding tables.
me: The paper evaluates three protection strategies: (1) linear scan of the embedding table (accesses all rows, hiding which row is used); (2) ORAM protection with optimized implementation; and (3) Deep Hash Embedding (DHE), which replaces the table lookup entirely with a hash-based neural network computation that takes the embedding index as input and produces an embedding vector through compute rather than memory access, eliminating the memory access pattern. A hybrid scheme combines DHE for large embedding tables (where its compute cost is amortized) with linear scan for small tables, selected per table based on profiled break-even points.
nv: Replacing embedding table lookups with compute-based DHE (Deep Hash Embedding) as a side-channel protection mechanism, which eliminates the memory access pattern rather than obfuscating it, yielding 4x performance improvement over optimized ORAM with up to 1116x memory footprint reduction.

mx.speedup: 4x for large DLRM embedding tables vs ORAM; up to 3.08x end-to-end vs optimized ORAM; 1.32x prefill and 1.07x decoding for GPT-2 vs ORAM
mx.other: Up to 1116x memory footprint reduction

th: compute-based DHE as memory side-channel protection for embedding table lookups

t: DPUaudit: DPU-assisted Pull-based Architecture for Near-Zero Cost System Auditing
pb: Existing hardware-based system auditing frameworks offload log processing to isolated hardware but still suffer high runtime overhead (>10% slowdown) because they use a push-based architecture requiring a log sender to run on the monitored host, which necessitates heavy software protection mechanisms that consume significant CPU resources.
me: DPUaudit replaces the push-based log sender on the monitored host with a pull-based architecture using a DPU (Data Processing Unit/SmartNIC) to actively pull system events directly from the monitored host's memory over the network interconnect. By removing the log sender from the monitored host entirely, DPUaudit eliminates the need for complex software protection mechanisms guarding it, achieving near-zero overhead. The DPU handles log collection, processing, and integrity verification in an isolated SmartNIC environment, physically separated from the monitored host.
nv: Inverting the auditing data flow from host-pushed to DPU-pulled, which eliminates the log sender on the monitored host and its associated protection overhead, achieving at most 2.1% runtime overhead versus one order-of-magnitude higher overhead in prior work.

mx.other: Average 2.1% runtime overhead (vs at least 10x higher in existing approaches) for 6 data center application workloads

th: DPU pull-based system auditing for near-zero overhead intrusion detection

t: SpecMPK: Efficient In-Process Isolation with Speculative and Secure Permission Update Instruction
pb: Memory Protection Keys (MPK) enable user-space access control for in-process isolation, but the permission update instruction (WRPKRU) is serialized, imposing significant performance overhead when applications require frequent domain switches to enforce isolation of critical data and pointers.
me: SpecMPK speculatively executes the MPK permission update instruction (WRPKRU) out-of-order rather than serializing it. A lightweight microarchitecture enhancement monitors all subsequent memory instructions that follow a speculative permission update: any instruction that would access a memory region whose permission was transiently upgraded (i.e., a potential speculative access to protected data) is blocked from committing until the permission update instruction itself becomes non-squashable (i.e., past the point of no return in the ROB). This prevents transient permission upgrades from being exploited by speculative execution attacks while allowing the processor to overlap permission update latency with useful computation.
nv: Allowing speculative out-of-order execution of WRPKRU while preventing speculative access to transiently upgraded memory regions through a blocking mechanism tied to the instruction's non-squashable commit point.

mx.speedup: Average 12.21% performance improvement for frequent-domain-switch SPEC workloads vs serialized WRPKRU

th: speculative MPK permission update for low-overhead in-process isolation

t: Chronus: Understanding and Securing the Cutting-Edge Industry Solutions to DRAM Read Disturbance
pb: The DDR5 Per Row Activation Counting (PRAC) RowHammer mitigation introduces non-trivial DRAM access latency overhead (counter increment in critical path) and is vulnerable to the 'wave attack' adversarial pattern, forcing overly conservative refresh thresholds that degrade performance.
me: Chronus is an on-DRAM-die RowHammer mitigation that separates activation counters from data arrays, allowing counter updates to proceed concurrently with data accesses (eliminating the latency penalty). It also dynamically controls the number of preventive refreshes issued per back-off signal to neutralize the wave attack — which forces repeated activation bursts to exhaust a fixed-refresh budget. The mechanism requires only in-DRAM modifications and is open-sourced.
nv: Decoupling activation counters from data storage arrays enables concurrent counter updates during memory accesses, eliminating PRAC's critical-path latency penalty while dynamic refresh count control defeats wave attacks.

mx.speedup: Near-zero performance overhead for modern DRAM chips; very low overhead for future chips
mx.other: Outperforms 3 PRAC variants and 3 other state-of-the-art read disturbance solutions

th: On-DRAM-die RowHammer mitigation with concurrent counter updates and adaptive refresh

t: NVMePass: A Lightweight, High-performance and Scalable NVMe Virtualization Architecture with I/O Queues Passthrough
pb: Existing NVMe virtualization approaches either suffer severe performance degradation (Virtio software path) or require dedicated hardware with limited VM scalability (VFIO/SR-IOV hardware passthrough). No solution simultaneously achieves near-native I/O performance, zero CPU overhead, and high VM count scalability.
me: NVMePass is a software-hardware co-design that passes NVMe I/O queues directly to VMs, enabling VMs to submit commands and receive completions without hypervisor involvement. DMA and interrupt remapping are handled without hypervisor interposition. A new hardware primitive, the NVMe Resource Domain (NRD), is implemented in the NVMe controller to enforce VM-level isolation by intercepting illegal I/O requests. Logical block address ranges and I/O queues are exclusively allocated per VM for isolation without per-operation hypervisor overhead.
nv: NVMe Resource Domain (NRD) implemented in the NVMe controller hardware enforces VM isolation at the storage device level, enabling full I/O queue passthrough without any hypervisor involvement in the data path.

mx.speedup: 40% lower latency vs. SPDK-Vhost at 150 VMs; 68% IOPS improvement vs. SPDK-Vhost in real-world app at 100 VMs
mx.other: 100.1-100.5% IOPS of VFIO (near-native)

th: Hardware-assisted NVMe I/O queue passthrough virtualization with in-device VM isolation

t: BrokenSleep: Remote Power Timing Attack Exploiting Processor Idle States
pb: Modern processors support multiple C-state (idle) levels with different wake-up latencies; an attacker can remotely detect which C-state a victim processor core is in by measuring network response timing, enabling covert and side-channel communication across nodes without requiring co-location on the same machine.
me: BrokenSleep exploits the deterministic wake-up latency differences between processor C-states (C0 active, C1/C1E/C6 sleep) to encode information in the timing of network responses from a victim server. The attacker sends network requests and measures response latency; the victim's current C-state (determined by its workload idle pattern) is deduced from the latency profile. Both covert channel (data exfiltration across security boundaries without direct network access) and side-channel (keystroke timing inference) variants are demonstrated. The attack affects both Intel and ARM processors, exploiting standard ACPI power management without any microarchitectural vulnerability.
nv: The first remote timing attack based purely on processor idle-state (C-state) wake-up latency differences, eliminating the co-location requirement of all prior power-based side-channel attacks.

mx.other: Demonstrated covert channel and keystroke timing inference over external network on Intel and ARM CPUs

th: remote C-state-based timing side-channel attack

t: Let-Me-In: (Still) Employing In-pointer Bounds Metadata for Fine-grained GPU Memory Safety
pb: GPU programs written in C/C++ inherit memory safety vulnerabilities such as out-of-bounds accesses. The heterogeneous GPU memory hierarchy (heap, local memory, thousands of concurrent threads) makes it difficult to enforce fine-grained bounds checking with low overhead.
me: LMI aligns GPU memory allocations to powers-of-two boundaries and performs static analysis at compile time to identify and mark pointer arithmetic instructions. Bounds metadata (base and size) is encoded into the unused upper bits of 64-bit GPU virtual address pointers, eliminating separate metadata memory structures. Hardware bounds-checking logic validates each memory access against the in-pointer metadata before issuing the request, adding minimal per-access latency even under thousands of concurrent threads.
nv: Storing per-object bounds metadata entirely within the unused upper bits of GPU pointers, made feasible by power-of-two allocation alignment and static pointer-arithmetic tagging, eliminating separate metadata tables and their associated overhead.

mx.other: negligible performance overhead vs baseline GPU execution

th: fine-grained GPU memory safety via in-pointer metadata

t: AutoRFM: Scaling Low-Cost in-DRAM Trackers to Ultra-Low Rowhammer Thresholds
pb: In-DRAM Rowhammer mitigation using the DDR5 Refresh Management (RFM) command stalls the entire DRAM bank for 200-400ns per invocation; at ultra-low Rowhammer thresholds (sub-100), the required RFM frequency causes up to 33% performance slowdown with existing low-cost trackers such as MINT.
me: AutoRFM performs transparent RFM at the subarray granularity rather than the full bank level: it targets only one subarray at a time for mitigation while all other subarrays continue to service requests uninterrupted. If an activation request arrives for the subarray currently under mitigation, the DRAM chip issues an ALERT signal to the Memory Controller to retry after a bounded 200ns wait. Randomized Memory Mapping breaks spatial correlation between consecutive bank accesses to prevent repeated targeting of the same subarray. A Fractal Mitigation Algorithm handles transitive Rowhammer attacks (e.g., Half-Double) without recursive same-subarray mitigations. The design is evaluated with SPEC, GAP, and stream workloads.
nv: Subarray-granularity transparent RFM that allows parallel servicing of non-targeted subarrays during mitigation, breaking the bank-level stall bottleneck of standard RFM.

mx.other: 3.1% average slowdown at Rowhammer threshold 74; vs 33% slowdown with bank-level RFM at threshold 100

th: subarray-granularity RFM for scalable in-DRAM Rowhammer mitigation

t: Understanding RowHammer Under Reduced Refresh Latency: Experimental Analysis of Real DRAM Chips and Implications on Future Solutions
pb: RowHammer mitigations based on preventive refresh incur growing performance and energy overheads as DRAM technology scaling reduces the activation threshold for bit-flip induction. The interaction between refresh latency and RowHammer vulnerability in real DRAM chips has not been rigorously characterized.
me: The authors perform the first experimental characterization of refresh-latency vs. RowHammer interactions on 388 real DDR4 chips from three manufacturers, varying preventive refresh (tRFM) latency below nominal values. They find that refresh latency can be reduced by 64% with only a 0.54% increase in required refresh count. Building on these findings, they design PaCRAM (Partial Charge Restoration for Aggressive Mitigation), a mechanism that reduces tRFM for preventive refreshes and compensates by slightly increasing refresh frequency, thus lowering the performance tax of five state-of-the-art RowHammer defenses.
nv: First silicon-validated demonstration that preventive DRAM refresh latency can be substantially reduced (by 64%) with minimal extra refresh count, enabling a new low-cost operating point for RowHammer mitigation.

mx.other: Refresh latency reduced by 64%; preventive refresh count increase of only 0.54%; performance and energy improvements over 5 state-of-the-art mitigations

th: RowHammer mitigation via reduced refresh latency

t: QPRAC: Towards Secure and Practical PRAC-based Rowhammer Mitigation using Priority Queues
pb: The JEDEC PRAC (Per Row Activation Counting) framework for DDR5 enables RowHammer mitigation via Alert Back-Off (ABO) signaling, but existing PRAC implementations (e.g., Panopticon) are either insecure when instantiated per JEDEC specification, or impractical (e.g., UPRAC) due to requiring oracle knowledge of the top-N most-activated rows.
me: QPRAC designs a Priority-based Service Queue (PSQ) in the memory controller that maintains pending mitigation requests sorted by row activation count, using PRAC's per-row counters to prioritize mitigations. High activation-count rows are served first, preventing adversarial bypass. The PSQ is co-designed with two complementary mechanisms: opportunistic mitigation during Refresh Management (RFM) operations (piggybacking extra mitigations at low cost), and proactive mitigation during standard DRAM refresh (REF) operations to drain the queue before ABO events fire, minimizing performance impact.
nv: A priority-based service queue (PSQ) that orders RowHammer mitigations by activation count within the PRAC/ABO framework, providing principled security while opportunistic and proactive refresh co-design reduces ABO-induced slowdowns to near zero.

mx.speedup: 0.8% slowdown for benign workloads (0% with proactive mitigations) at threshold=71

th: Priority-queue-based secure RowHammer mitigation for PRAC/ABO DDR5

t: DAPPER: A Performance-Attack-Resilient Tracker for RowHammer Defense
pb: Host-side RowHammer mitigation mechanisms rely on shared counter or tracking structures that are vulnerable to Performance Attacks (Perf-Attacks), where adversaries reverse-engineer the shared structure's mapping to artificially inflate DRAM access counters or trigger early resets, degrading performance of co-running benign applications.
me: DAPPER introduces secure hashing to randomize the mapping of DRAM rows to shared tracking structures, preventing adversaries from predicting counter locations. DAPPER-S provides a base secure hashing template using a single hash function. DAPPER-H extends this with double-hashing, novel reset strategies that avoid predictable early resets, and mitigative refresh techniques that piggyback RowHammer mitigations onto scheduled refresh operations to amortize overhead. The combined design uses only 96KB of SRAM per 32GB of DRAM, validated against 57 workloads from SPEC2006, SPEC2017, TPC, Hadoop, MediaBench, and YCSB.
nv: Secure double-hashing with adaptive reset strategies that simultaneously thwart RowHammer bit-flip attacks and Perf-Attacks on shared tracking structures, using under 100KB SRAM per 32GB DRAM.

mx.speedup: 0.9% slowdown under Perf-Attacks at threshold=500

th: Perf-Attack-resilient RowHammer tracking via secure hashing and double-hash reset strategies

t: Palermo: Improving the Performance of Oblivious Memory using Protocol-Hardware Co-Design
pb: Oblivious RAM (ORAM) protocols impose severe performance penalties because classical ORAM enforces strict sequential dependencies between memory operations, leaving memory bandwidth severely underutilized. Prior prefetching and request-elimination approaches are fragile under low-locality workloads and create additional ORAM stash pressure overhead.
me: Palermo redesigns the RingORAM protocol to allow overlapping of memory operations both within a single ORAM request and across multiple concurrent requests, without violating correctness or security invariants. A dedicated ORAM controller hardware implements this relaxed protocol by concurrently issuing memory requests while tracking and enforcing only the necessary inter-request dependencies to maintain a consistent ORAM tree view. The architecture manages stash and position-map structures in hardware to prevent stash overflow while enabling pipelined DRAM accesses.
nv: A protocol-hardware co-design that removes artificial sequential constraints in classical ORAM, enabling concurrent multi-request memory access without breaking security or correctness guarantees.

mx.speedup: 2.9x over RingORAM baseline
mx.area: 5.78mm^2 ORAM controller (<2% overhead in 12th-gen Intel CPU after technology scaling)
mx.other: 2.14W power; outperforms PageORAM, PrORAM, IR-ORAM

th: ORAM protocol-hardware co-design for bandwidth-efficient secure memory

t: Everything Depends on Your Hammer: A Systematic Rowhammer Attack Exploration on SPHINCS+
pb: Post-quantum cryptographic implementations are vulnerable to rowhammer-based fault injection attacks on native systems, where remote attackers can forge digital signatures.
me: Characterize the DRAM fault model on specific platforms (DDR3/DDR4), then devise optimal rowhammer attacks by analyzing fault patterns. Demonstrate a forgery attack on SPHINCS+ using rowhammer on standard liboqs implementation.
nv: First rowhammer-based forgery attack on SPHINCS+ (NIST standard), demonstrating practical fault injection threats for hash-based digital signatures in cloud systems.

mx.other: demonstrated on DDR3 and DDR4 DRAM

th: fault-based PQC attack via rowhammer

t: MIRAGE: Microarchitectural Footprints for Detecting Adversarial Attacks in One-Shot Inference
pb: Detecting adversarial attacks on DNNs in resource-constrained systems requires expensive defenses; existing HPC-based detection requires state cleaning between inferences, degrading system performance.
me: MIRAGE uses hardware performance counters without requiring cache/branch predictor state cleaning. CNN classifier trained on HPC signals detects adversarial samples in single inference.
nv: One-shot adversarial detection using HPCs without state cleaning, enabling practical online deployment with full hardware optimization.

mx.other: 60ms timing overhead, maintains high throughput

th: one-shot adversarial detection via HPC

t: "Energon": Unveiling Transformers from GPU Power and Thermal Side-Channels
pb: GPU power and thermal fluctuations leak architectural details of transformer models deployed in MLaaS environments, enabling extraction of layer counts and attention head information without physical access.
me: Exploits temporal variations in GPU power consumption and thermal output via unprivileged access to extract architectural parameters; analyzes encoder/decoder layers and attention head counts through statistical power signatures.
nv: First demonstration of GPU power and thermal side-channels to reverse-engineer transformer architecture details at user privilege level.

mx.accuracy: 89% model family identification, 100% hyperparameter classification, 93% adversarial success
mx.other: Works in single-process and noisy multi-process scenarios

th: Transformer security via GPU side-channels

t: Designing with Deception: ML- and Covert Gate-Enhanced Camouflaging to Thwart IC Reverse Engineering
pb: Integrated circuits face significant security risks from physical reverse engineering attacks; existing IC camouflaging focuses on localized gate modifications without comprehensive deception strategies.
me: Presents ML-driven IP Camouflage methodology using And-Inverter Graph Variational Autoencoder (AIG-VAE) for circuit representation encoding, enabling dual-layered camouflage through functional preservation and appearance mimicry via novel covert gates (Fake Inverters, Fake Buffers, Universal Transmitters).
nv: ML-based dual-layered camouflage combining functional deception via circuit modification and appearance deception via covert gate insertion.

mx.other: Maintains circuit functionality under camouflage

th: ML-based circuit camouflaging

t: JitFilt: Mitigate Jitter-based Side Channel Analysis Attacks
pb: Signal jitter emanating from cryptographic circuits can be exploited via jitter-based side-channel analysis (JitSCA) attacks using time-to-digital converters to conduct remote attacks.
me: Signal jitter filter implementation using FPGA mixed-mode clock managers (MMCMs), phase-locked loops (PLLs), and IDELAY components to reduce signal jitter in cryptographic designs.
nv: First countermeasure specifically designed to mitigate jitter-based side-channel analysis attacks on cryptographic hardware.

mx.other: protection: 166x traces improvement (5M vs 30k)

th: First countermeasure for jitter-based side-channel attacks

t: Defense in the Reverse Fragment: RL-Based Partial Netlist Hardware Trojan Detection
pb: Hardware Trojan detection methods assume complete netlists, but practical reverse engineering yields incomplete/partial information, reducing detection accuracy and stability.
me: RE-PNRL: Reinforcement Learning-based framework for reconstructing partial netlists using node-level transition probabilities. Clustering-based hardware Trojan detection using complete netlist reconstruction.
nv: First hardware Trojan detection framework addressing practical partial-netlist scenarios from reverse engineering.

mx.other: Robust across netlist missingness levels

th: RL-based hardware trojan detection with partial netlist information

t: RTPU: Unifying Non-Private and Private Inference with Reconfigurable Architecture
pb: Data centers must simultaneously handle plaintext-based non-private inference and ciphertext-based private inference (via fully homomorphic encryption), but current solutions require costly dedicated accelerators or inflexible general-purpose hardware with poor performance.
me: RTPU reconfigurable architecture exploits inherent similarities between plaintext tensor and polynomial ring ciphertext computations through fine-grained reconfiguration. Kernel group-based scheduling optimizes hardware utilization and QoS across multi-tenant workloads with varying privacy requirements.
nv: Reconfigurable multi-core architecture that seamlessly switches between tensor-based plaintext and polynomial ring-based ciphertext computations with substantial silicon reuse.

mx.other: High resource utilization for multi-tenant workloads

th: Reconfigurable accelerator for private and non-private inference

t: Secure Token Pruning Mechanism and Accelerator for Vision Transformer
pb: Vision Transformers are vulnerable to adversarial patch attacks; existing defense strategies improve robustness but incur significant computational overhead, limiting practical deployment in security-critical applications.
me: STEM defense integrates Block-wise Selective Fusion (BSF) to fuse redundant and flag suspicious tokens, and Identify-Prune (IP) to remove adversarial tokens based on multi-head attention statistics. STEMA accelerator features dedicated Security Core with token fusion, top-k selection, and metadata engines (5% chip area).
nv: Parallelizable token pruning defense combining selective fusion and statistical pruning with dedicated hardware accelerator occupying minimal chip area.

mx.speedup: 46.8-105.8× vs. defense baselines; 71× via STEMA
mx.other: SOTA robustness performance

th: Secure and efficient Vision Transformer acceleration

t: SNO: Securing Network Function Offloading on FPGA-based SmartNICs in Untrusted Clouds
pb: FPGA-based SmartNICs offload network functions but lack security guarantees for untrusted clouds; existing FPGA TEEs fail to provide packet I/O protection and user-friendly memory access, forcing users to trust cloud service providers.
me: SNO introduces: (1) secure boot for FPGA TEE, (2) SNO Manager for attestation/orchestration with CPU TEE co-location, (3) SNO Guard with fully-pipelined AES-GCM engine for I/O encryption/authentication. Design enables overlapped execution reducing latency overhead.
nv: First TEE for FPGA-based SmartNICs combining secure boot, attestation, and I/O encryption with minimal performance overhead.

mx.other: 7.7-143.2% latency overhead; 86.9% code reduction

th: Secure SmartNIC network function offloading

t: Leaks beyond Bits: Deep Learning-Assisted Side-Channel Attacks on Hyperdimensional Computing Accelerators
pb: FPGA-based Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) accelerators are vulnerable to side-channel attacks that can extract stored hypervector bits, compromising security of edge/IoT applications.
me: Proposes a specialized CNN-based side-channel analysis (SCA) to extract hypervector bits, enhanced by adaptive Grad-CAM-guided approach that iteratively highlights critical leakage regions to improve signal-to-noise ratio and accelerate attacks. Includes dynamic masking countermeasure.
nv: CNN-based adaptive side-channel analysis with Grad-CAM guidance for HDC accelerator vulnerability.
th: CNN-based side-channel attacks on HDC accelerators

t: TREX-F: TRustability of Electronics using X-ray based Fingerprinting
pb: Counterfeit and tampered printed circuit boards (PCBs) infiltrate the electronics supply chain, posing risks to business and security.
me: TREX-F leverages inherent physical defects (solder irregularities, material deposition, microscopic anomalies) captured by X-ray microscopy at specific angles. Uses computer vision techniques (Canny edge detection, contour detection, PCA, SIFT) to extract unique fingerprints from X-ray CT slices, converting them into QR and data-matrix codes for authentication.
nv: X-ray-based physical fingerprinting for PCB authentication using computer vision analysis.
th: X-ray fingerprinting for PCB authentication

t: FlexTEE: Dynamically Enhancing Metadata Locality Through Affine Address Transformation for Heterogeneous & Secure AI Platforms
pb: DNN accelerators in heterogeneous secure AI platforms suffer from poor metadata locality when managing Merkle tree integrity structures, causing performance bottlenecks and security vulnerabilities.
me: Apply affine address transformations to dynamically optimize Merkle tree metadata layout in accelerator memory hierarchies. Adaptively reorganize tree structures to improve cache/scratchpad locality based on runtime access patterns in heterogeneous CPU-GPU systems.
nv: Dynamic metadata locality optimization via affine address transformation for Merkle tree integrity in secure heterogeneous AI accelerators.
th: metadata locality optimization for secure AI acceleration

t: Unveiling the Mask: Trusted Semiconductor Manufacturing through Wafer-Level Mask-Set Attestation
pb: Semiconductor supply chain security requires detecting wafers fabricated with untrusted mask-sets; traditional methods cannot leverage wafer metrology data for attestation.
me: Machine learning-based approach using inline and e-test measurements to capture subtle causality between mask modifications and physical/electrical characteristics from 8000 wafers.
nv: First ML-based wafer-level mask-set attestation exploiting process variation signatures.
th: Supply-chain security through wafer-level mask-set attestation

t: PATHE: A Privacy-Preserving Database Pattern Search Platform with Homomorphic Encryption
pb: Database pattern search requires sensitive data handling, raising privacy concerns in centralized query systems.
me: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) combined with Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) for encrypted search. CXL-based hardware accelerator for FHE/HDC co-processing. Demonstrated on protein spectra database queries.
nv: First FHE+HDC co-design accelerator for privacy-preserving database pattern search.
th: Privacy-preserving database search with FHE

t: FPGA-CC: Confidential Containers for Virtualized FPGAs
pb: Virtualized FPGA cloud services lack security mechanisms to protect user data and computation, as current trusted execution environment (TEE) approaches do not support FPGA acceleration in cloud environments.
me: Develops FPGA-CC, an end-to-end confidential container framework establishing a secure path between virtualized FPGA resources and TEE-based CPU containers. Provides isolated execution and secure data channels for virtual FPGA instances while enabling performance-acceptable operations.
nv: First confidential container framework enabling secure TEE integration with virtualized cloud FPGAs through secure path establishment between FPGA and TEE-CPU components.
th: Secure confidential containers for virtualized FPGAs

t: Uranus: Ultra-efficient Acceleration Architecture for the Privacy Inference of Graph Neural Networks
pb: Fully Homomorphic Encryption enables secure GNN inference on encrypted data, but high computational costs make it impractical without dedicated accelerators. Existing CKKS-based GNN approaches require large encryption parameters; PPGNN combines CKKS with TFHE for memory efficiency but TFHE's SISD computing causes severe computational overhead.
me: Proposes Uranus, a software-hardware co-designed GNN accelerator with: (1) inference framework leveraging CKKS for linear layers and BFV for SIMD-based nonlinear calculations with reduced encryption parameters suitable for hardware, and (2) highly reconfigurable hardware accelerator maximizing utilization. Combines multiple FHE schemes strategically to balance computation, memory, and accuracy requirements.
nv: First software-hardware co-designed FHE-based GNN accelerator achieving 92× speedup over CKKS-only and 3.3-4.2× over PPGNN with 119× energy efficiency improvement.
th: FHE-based privacy-preserving GNN accelerator

t: Non-Negative AdderNet: Algorithm-Hardware Co-design for Lightweight Defense of Adversarial Bit-Flip Attacks
pb: Neural networks are vulnerable to bit-flip attacks that corrupt computation. Traditional defense mechanisms add significant overhead, limiting deployment on resource-constrained devices.
me: Non-Negative AdderNet with hardware defense architecture using non-positive weight encoding and integrated decoder. Algorithm-hardware co-design minimizes overhead. Defends against adversarial bit-flip attacks with reduced complexity.
nv: Hardware-friendly non-negative adder networks with integrated bit-flip defense via non-positive weight encoding.
th: Bit-flip attack defense network

t: CacheGuardian: A Timing Side-Channel Resilient LLC Design
pb: The last-level cache (LLC) shared by multiple tenants in cloud computing is frequently exploited through timing side-channel attacks, enabling unauthorized data leakage. Existing defense mechanisms show deficiencies in performance overhead, attack coverage, and detection accuracy.
me: Hardware-based LLC protection featuring behavior-based, generic attack detector for real-time identification of multiple timing side-channel attacks and cache-set-level access control mechanism that restricts cache usage exclusively to identified attackers instead of influencing all security domains. Implemented and evaluated in gem5 simulator.
nv: Behavior-based generic attack detector with cache-set-level access control for granular, low-overhead timing side-channel defense.
th: Cache security against timing attacks

t: Adaptive CHERI Compartmentalization for Heterogeneous Accelerators
pb: Hardware accelerators in heterogeneous systems lack fine-grained memory protection: IOMMU-based isolation operates at page granularity, leaving intra-page accesses unprotected, while per-accelerator memory safety modifications require significant engineering effort and do not scale across diverse accelerator types.
me: CapChecker is an adaptive hardware interface inserted between CHERI-unaware accelerators and the system memory bus. It imports capability metadata from the CPU's CHERI register file and enforces pointer-level bounds and permission checks on every memory access issued by the accelerator, without modifying the accelerator architecture itself. The interface interposes on the accelerator's memory request channel, decodes the capability tag and bounds from the CPU-managed capability table, and raises a fault on any out-of-bounds or permission-violating access. Capability grants from the CPU are communicated through a lightweight descriptor mechanism that maps accelerator DMA addresses to CHERI capabilities.
nv: A general-purpose, accelerator-architecture-agnostic capability enforcement shim (CapChecker) that extends CHERI pointer-level memory protection to CHERI-unaware accelerators by importing CPU capabilities at the hardware interface, requiring zero accelerator modification.

mx.other: 1.4% average performance overhead vs. CHERI-unaware accelerators across benchmark set

th: CHERI capability extension to heterogeneous accelerators for fine-grained memory protection

t: SpecASan: Mitigating Transient Execution Attacks Using Speculative Address Sanitization
pb: Transient execution attacks (Spectre, Meltdown, MDS) exploit speculative execution to leak sensitive data through residual microarchitectural state, and existing defenses either delay speculative execution or require costly shadow structures and dynamic information flow tracking. Providing strong security against transient execution attacks without significant performance overhead remains an open problem.
me: SpecASan extends ARM's Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) from the committed path to the speculative path. When a speculative memory access fails the MTE tag comparison (i.e., the tag on the pointer does not match the tag in memory), that access is stalled until speculation resolves, preventing it from affecting microarchitectural state (caches, TLBs). This is combined with existing Control-Flow Integrity (CFI) enforcement to block gadget construction. The approach models transient execution attacks as software-defined security contract violations and enforces the contracts in hardware using existing MTE tag-check hardware, requiring minimal new hardware.
nv: SpecASan is the first design to repurpose ARM MTE tag checks on the speculative execution path to selectively delay potentially leaking memory accesses, enforcing security contracts without disabling speculation or adding shadow structures.

mx.other: Low performance overhead (exact number not given in abstract); coverage of Spectre + MDS

th: hardware-enforced transient execution attack mitigation via memory tagging

t: Cassandra: Efficient Enforcement of Sequential Execution for Cryptographic Programs
pb: Modern out-of-order processors violate constant-time programming assumptions by transiently executing unintended control-flow paths, enabling Spectre-class transient execution attacks against cryptographic code. Existing mitigations that address control-flow misspeculations impose high performance overhead by broadly restricting speculative execution.
me: Cassandra disables branch prediction for constant-time cryptographic code regions and instead records and replays the deterministic sequential control flow using a Branch Trace Unit (BTU) added to the processor. Exploiting the observation that constant-time programs have mostly static control flow across runs and that cryptographic programs are loop-intensive with highly compressible control-flow patterns, Cassandra performs upfront branch analysis to compress control-flow traces stored in the BTU. The BTU then supplies fetch redirections from compressed trace storage, bypassing speculative branch prediction entirely for protected code regions.
nv: Replacing the branch predictor with a record-and-replay mechanism using compressed control-flow traces for constant-time cryptographic code, achieving security without speculation overhead and even a net average speedup over an unsafe baseline.

mx.speedup: average 1.85% speedup over unsafe baseline processor
mx.other: strong security guarantee against Spectre-class transient execution attacks on constant-time code

th: secure sequential execution enforcement for constant-time cryptographic code

t: Single-Address-Space FaaS with Jord
pb: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) systems incur millisecond-level overheads from isolating functions in separate address spaces (containers or microVMs), preventing them from meeting microsecond-scale service-level objectives (SLOs) required by microservice workloads. The address-space isolation mechanism forces costly context switches, copy-on-write, and cross-function data copies.
me: Jord co-locates functions in a single address space using hardware/software co-design for user-level in-process memory isolation that extends traditional virtual memory capabilities. Memory isolation and protection are enforced at nanosecond granularity without kernel involvement by leveraging hardware memory protection keys or equivalent mechanisms, enabling zero-copy cross-function communication. Scalable function dispatch is achieved through user-level scheduling that avoids OS-level context switches, allowing Jord to meet microsecond SLOs.
nv: Jord revives the function-as-a-function FaaS semantic by enabling user-level in-process memory isolation at nanosecond granularity within a single address space, eliminating the container/microVM overhead that causes millisecond latencies.

mx.speedup: Over 2x throughput vs. enhanced state-of-the-art FaaS
mx.other: Within 16% of idealized insecure baseline; microsecond-level SLO achieved

th: Single-address-space FaaS with user-level in-process memory isolation

t: DREAM: Enabling Low-Overhead Rowhammer Mitigation via Directed Refresh Management
pb: JEDEC's Directed Refresh Management (DRFM) commands stall 8–32 DRAM banks simultaneously during Rowhammer mitigation, causing severe performance overheads (up to 49% slowdown) compared to the per-bank NRR assumed by prior work. Existing counter-based trackers that avoid these stalls require impractically large storage.
me: DREAM proposes two DRFM-aware variants. DREAM-R (randomized) delays issuing a DRFM after sampling an aggressor row so that other banks can also sample rows within the same window, amortizing the multi-bank stall across more mitigations per DRFM command. DREAM-C (counter-based) groups 32–256 randomly chosen rows across 32 banks into a 'gang' that shares a single counter, reducing tracker storage by 8x versus Graphene while avoiding CAM lookups and preserving DRFM compatibility.
nv: Exploiting DRFM's inherent multi-bank parallelism to either batch-amortize stalls (DREAM-R) or dramatically compress tracker storage via gang counting (DREAM-C), without requiring non-standard DRAM commands.

mx.speedup: DREAM-R reduces PARA slowdown from 12.7% to 4.24% (DRFMsb); DREAM-C reduces storage to 1 KB/bank (8x vs Graphene) with negligible slowdown at threshold 500
mx.other: PARA with NRR: 3.9% slowdown; with DRFMab: 49% slowdown (baselines)

th: DRAM Rowhammer mitigation with JEDEC DRFM

t: MoPAC: Efficiently Mitigating Rowhammer with Probabilistic Activation Counting
pb: DDR5 JEDEC's Per-Row Activation Counters (PRAC) introduce extended DRAM timing parameters that cause 10% average performance overhead for all applications—even benign ones—because counter updates are performed on every activation regardless of actual attack likelihood.
me: MoPAC reduces counter-update frequency by performing PRAC updates probabilistically rather than on every row activation. To maintain security, the mitigation threshold is adjusted downward by the inverse of the sampling probability to ensure aggressors are still caught before exceeding the Rowhammer threshold. MoPAC-C (memory-controller side) uses two precharge command variants: a normal-latency precharge that skips counter updates and a higher-latency precharge that performs counter updates, with the controller probabilistically selecting which to issue. MoPAC-D (in-DRAM) probabilistically selects activations for counter updates within the DRAM chip and uses ALERT or REF timing to absorb the counter-update latency.
nv: Probabilistic PRAC counter updates with threshold compensation, enabling a hardware-transparent reduction in DDR5 timing overhead while preserving formal Rowhammer security guarantees.

mx.speedup: MoPAC-C: 1.7% slowdown; MoPAC-D: 0.7% slowdown at threshold 500 vs. 10% for PRAC

th: Probabilistic DRAM activation counting for efficient Rowhammer mitigation

t: When Mitigations Backfire: Timing Channel Attacks and Defense for PRAC-Based RowHammer Mitigations
pb: The JEDEC DDR5 Per Row Activation Counting (PRAC) mechanism and its Alert Back-Off (ABO) protocol and Refresh Management (RFM) commands introduce observable timing differences that create a new timing side-channel, allowing attackers to monitor memory access latencies and infer sensitive information such as cryptographic keys.
me: The paper first presents PRACLeak, a timing channel attack that exploits latency variations induced by ABO protocol and RFM commands to extract secret keys from vulnerable AES implementations by monitoring memory access timing. To counter this, the authors propose Timing-Safe PRAC (TPRAC), which replaces activity-triggered RFM commands with Timing-Based RFMs issued periodically and independently of memory activity, eliminating the observable correlation between memory access patterns and mitigation timing. TPRAC requires only a single-entry in-DRAM mitigation queue per bank and is designed to be compatible with existing DRAM standards.
nv: Identification of a timing side-channel in PRAC's ABO+RFM signaling and a defense (TPRAC) that decouples mitigation timing from memory activity using periodic, activity-independent RFM issuance.

mx.other: 3.4% performance overhead at Rowhammer threshold 1024 for TPRAC

th: timing side-channel in PRAC Rowhammer mitigation and a safe fix

t: An Eye-Opening Arbiter PUF for Fingerprint Generation Using Auto-Error Detection for PVT-Robust Masking and Bit Stabilization Achieving a BER of 2e-8 in 28nm CMOS
pb: Physically unclonable functions (PUFs) for hardware identification and key generation must maintain constant fingerprint across voltage, temperature, and time variations while minimizing bit error rate (BER), but prior techniques either sacrifice speed/area for low BER via averaging/masking or rely on shared/off-chip error-correction hardware with security risks.
me: Arbiter-PUF design combining auto-error-detection circuitry with PVT-robust masking to stabilize bit readout across environmental variations, achieving BER of 2e-8 in 28nm CMOS without large error-correction overhead.
nv: Auto-error-detection mechanism enabling on-chip PVT-robust masking and bit stabilization without off-chip or shared error-correction, reducing security risk and area.
th: Low-BER arbiter PUF with on-chip error detection.

t: A Single-Link Multi-Domain-Output (SLiMDO) Isolated DC-DC Converter with Passive Magnetic Flux Sharing for Local Energy Distribution and Rx Behavior Sensing-Based Global Power Modulation
pb: Galvanically isolated DC-DC converters with multiple domain-specific outputs require separate control signals across isolation barriers and custom interconnect topologies, increasing complexity and requiring digital isolators for Tx-Rx communication.
me: Single-link topology using passive magnetic flux sharing and receiver-side behavior sensing for global power modulation, eliminating need for digital isolators and enabling flexible domain-specific output configuration.
nv: Passive magnetic flux sharing with Rx-side sensing-based global power modulation eliminating cross-isolation control signals.
th: Multi-domain isolated power delivery with passive control

t: An Efficient Vth-Tilting PUF Design in 3nm GAA and 8nm FinFET Technologies
pb: Physically unclonable functions require process-mismatch entropy extraction while maintaining stability across process-voltage-temperature corners; conventional PUF enrollment requires screening across multiple PVT conditions, increasing test time and cost.
me: Standard-cell-only PUF extracting entropy from threshold-voltage mismatches in inverting cells, with Vth-tilting scheme supporting efficient enrollment by screening at nominal V/T only; includes power-gating (BTI mitigation), balanced sampler (side-channel reduction), and laser-attack detection.
nv: Vth-tilting enrollment scheme enabling efficient screening at nominal conditions only, reducing EDS test time.
th: Efficient PUF with optimized enrollment for hardware security

t: 17.3 A 30.4GOPS/mW MK-CKKS Processor for Secure Multi-Party Computation
pb: Multi-key fully homomorphic encryption (MK-FHE) processors for secure multi-party computation face challenges in integrating flexible configuration of task-, ciphertext-, and polynomial-level operations into a single area-efficient hardware architecture that scales to an unlimited number of parties.
me: The processor implements a flexible, scalable architecture for MK-CKKS that supports variable task-level configurations (linear/nonlinear transformations) composed from ciphertext-level operations (multiplication, key-switching, rescaling) and polynomial-level operations (NTT, base conversion, permutations) optimized for area efficiency.
nv: First hardware processor supporting MK-CKKS for unlimited-party multi-party computation with flexible integration of hierarchical operation combinations.
th: Hardware acceleration for multi-key fully homomorphic encryption

t: 17.6 A 100MHz Self-Calibrating RC Oscillator Capable of Clock-Glitch Detection for Hardware Security in a 3nm FinFET Process
pb: On-chip oscillators are needed for SoC security functions (boot-up, external clock attack detection), but existing designs either provide stable clocks without glitch detection or detect glitches without maintaining stability—no prior design achieves both.
me: Self-calibrating RC oscillator in 3nm FinFET with dual-mode operation: stable 100MHz clock generation via self-calibration and hardware-integrated clock-glitch detection circuit that can identify fault injection attacks on critical system clocks.
nv: First RC oscillator design combining stable on-chip clock generation with integrated clock-glitch detection in a single validated security IP, enabling both boot-up independence and real-time attack monitoring.

mx.other: 100MHz stable oscillation, glitch detection capability

th: Unified on-chip oscillator for stable clocking and security attack detection

t: An Enhanced-Frequency-Splitting-Based Wireless Power and Data Transfer System Achieving 60.2% End-to-End Efficiency and 1 Mb/s Data Rate with a Sub-cm RX Coil for Miniaturized Implants
pb: Miniaturized implantable devices face a fundamental trade-off between power transfer efficiency (PTE) and data rate (DR) in wireless power and data transfer (WPDT) systems, worsened by coil size constraints; frequency-splitting-based WPDT reduces this trade-off but still requires large receiver coils to achieve critical coupling coefficient, limiting implant miniaturization.
me: Enhanced-frequency-splitting WPDT (EFS-WPDT) system with dynamically controlled receiver LC tank enables Frequency Splitting Enhancement (FSE). By implementing link-load isolation (LLI) via switched on-resistance, the link sees lower effective load resistance, reducing critical coupling coefficient proportionally to loaded receiver Q. Dual-frequency flat-region FSK (FR-FSK) operation at frequencies f_H and f_L maintains both power transfer and data modulation while dynamic LLI enables efficient operation even with sub-cm receiver coils.
nv: Dynamic link-load isolation via switchable receiver tank achieving 10x coil-size reduction while maintaining frequency-splitting efficiency benefits.
th: dynamic link-load isolation for coil-size-reduced wireless implant power transfer

t: 35.4: A Miniature Biomedical Implant Secured by Two-Factor Authentication with Emergency Access
pb: Ensuring secure access to implantable medical devices (IMDs) while enabling emergency responders to bypass standard authentication when a doctor's account is compromised or unavailable.
me: Implements two-factor authentication with an emergency override mechanism that allows responders without server-stored pre-shared keys (PSKs) to access IMDs during emergencies, addressing both credential compromise and connectivity failures.
nv: Two-factor authentication scheme with built-in emergency access that does not require access to the PSK server.

mx.other: emergency access time, security level

th: Secure IMD access with emergency override

t: 17.1: Sensor-Less Laser Voltage-Probing Attack Detection via Run-Time-Leakage-Shift Monitoring with 4.35% Area Overhead
pb: Laser voltage probing (LVP) attacks on integrated circuits achieve near-100% success rate by probing on-chip voltages through backside laser illumination with high spatial resolution and low cost. Current detection approaches lack effective sensor-less mechanisms to counter these physical attacks in cost-constrained systems.
me: The design uses run-time leakage-shift monitoring to detect laser-induced anomalies without dedicated attack sensors. By observing shifts in device leakage currents caused by photocurrent injection during LVP attacks, the circuit can trigger countermeasures with minimal area overhead (4.35%).
nv: Sensor-less detection of LVP attacks exploiting run-time leakage-shift signatures without requiring photodiodes or dedicated sensing infrastructure.

mx.other: attack detection coverage near 100%

th: Sensor-less hardware security via leakage monitoring

t: CryptoBTB: A Secure Hierarchical BTB for Diverse Instruction Footprint Workloads
pb: Branch Target Buffer (BTB) timing attacks allow adversaries to infer victim BTB updates and mistrain branch predictors, bypassing privilege-level isolation and secure enclave protection; existing encrypted BTB schemes either have security weaknesses or encrypt the BTB index in-pipeline, exposing high latency.
me: CryptoBTB proposes a hierarchical exclusive BTB structure where the index encryption is decoupled from the BTB set index computation. The encryption step uses a low-latency scheme that obscures the set mapping without being on the critical prediction path; the hierarchical organization (L1 BTB + L2 BTB) avoids the collision-prone flat structure of prior work (HyBP), allowing the BTB capacity to be better utilized for workloads with large instruction footprints and reducing same-thread collisions.
nv: Decoupling the index encryption from the BTB indexing path enables low-latency secure BTB access while the hierarchical exclusive design recovers the BTB utilization lost by prior schemes that only partially utilize capacity.

mx.speedup: 4.27% performance overhead (vs. 31.89% for HyBP)

th: secure hierarchical BTB with decoupled low-latency index encryption

t: Understanding and Mitigating Covert Channel and Side Channel Vulnerabilities Introduced by RowHammer Defenses
pb: Modern RowHammer defenses (PRAC, RFM) introduce timing covert and side channels because their preventive refresh actions block DRAM access in ways that depend on application memory access patterns, allowing adversaries to both observe victim access behavior and establish covert communication channels. No prior work has analyzed these defense-induced timing vulnerabilities.
me: The paper introduces LeakyHammer, a class of attacks exploiting the timing latency increase caused by RowHammer preventive refresh actions. Two covert channels are built: one exploiting PRAC's per-row activation counter responses and one exploiting RFM's refresh management commands, both causing measurable DRAM latency spikes observable by a spy process. A proof-of-concept website fingerprinting attack identifies visited websites by correlating RowHammer-preventive action patterns triggered by a victim's browsing. Three countermeasures (randomized refresh scheduling, access pattern obfuscation, and noise injection) are evaluated.
nv: First systematic demonstration that RowHammer defense mechanisms themselves (PRAC and RFM) can be weaponized as covert and side channels via defense-induced DRAM bandwidth throttling.

mx.other: Covert channel capacity: 39.0 Kbps (PRAC), 48.7 Kbps (RFM)

th: RowHammer defense-induced timing side and covert channels

t: ρHammer: Reviving RowHammer Attacks on New Architectures via Prefetching
pb: Conventional load-based (MOV instruction) RowHammer attacks have become ineffective on the most recent Intel architectures (Alder Lake / Raptor Lake, 12th–14th gen), where load-based hammering produces zero bit flips, primarily because insufficient DRAM row activation rates and more aggressive out-of-order/speculative execution disrupt the attack's hammering order.
me: ρHammer introduces three coordinated techniques: (1) A layout-agnostic DRAM address mapping reverse-engineering algorithm using selective pairwise SBDR (Same-Bank Different-Row) timing measurements in a three-step Duet/Trios/Quartet structured deduction that recovers full bank functions in polynomial time without prior knowledge of bank bit counts or layouts; (2) A prefetch-based hammering paradigm exploiting the asynchronous nature of x86 PREFETCHT2/PREFETCHNTA instructions, which retire after forwarding to L1 LFB without stalling the CPU, combined with multi-bank parallelism to maximize per-tREFI activation rate while also alleviating disorder through bank-interleaving latency; (3) A counter-speculation technique using runtime control-flow obfuscation (indirect addressing) and NOP-based pseudo-barriers tuned to neutralize OoO execution and branch prediction reordering without using explicit memory barriers, which cannot order prefetch instructions per Intel SDM.
nv: A prefetch-based Rowhammer hammering paradigm that exploits the asynchronous, non-blocking nature of x86 software prefetch instructions to bypass load-based activation rate bottlenecks, enabling the first successful RowHammer attacks on Raptor Lake where all prior methods completely fail.

mx.other: flip rate: 187K/min on Comet Lake (112.4x over load baseline); 47K/min on Rocket Lake (47.1x over baseline); 2,291/min on Raptor Lake (baseline: 0); 200K+ bit flips in 2-hour fuzzing on Comet Lake

th: Prefetch-based RowHammer revival on modern Intel architectures

t: ShadowBinding: Realizing Effective Microarchitectures for In-Core Secure Speculation Schemes
pb: Secure speculation schemes that mitigate Spectre-class speculative side-channel attacks (such as STT and NDA) lack rigorous RTL-level microarchitectural implementations and realistic performance/cost analysis, causing prior work to significantly underestimate their overhead. Specifically, STT's rename-stage taint computation creates an expensive single-cycle dependency chain that degrades performance on wider out-of-order cores.
me: ShadowBinding develops concrete RTL microarchitectures for two state-of-the-art secure speculation schemes—Speculative Taint Tracking (STT) and Non-Speculative Data Access (NDA)—implemented on the RISC-V Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine (BOOM). For STT, a novel variant called STT-Issue is proposed that delays taint computation from the rename stage to the issue stage, breaking the expensive single-cycle rename-stage dependency chain and improving IPC, area, and timing. RTL synthesis and cycle-accurate simulation are used to measure the combined IPC and timing impact, capturing the full performance loss including clock frequency degradation.
nv: STT-Issue delays taint propagation to the issue stage, eliminating the rename-stage dependency chain that limits performance for wide cores, and is the first RTL-backed evaluation revealing that combined IPC+timing overhead of in-core secure speculation exceeds 35% for high-performance cores.

mx.other: IPC impact ~20% for highest-performance core; combined IPC+timing loss: 35% (STT-Rename), 27% (STT-Issue), 22% (NDA)

th: microarchitectural cost of in-core secure speculation

t: Efficient Security Support for CXL Memory through Adaptive Incremental Offloaded (Re-)Encryption
pb: CXL memory expansion devices adopted in cloud TEE environments (Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV) require XTS encryption for data confidentiality via CXL IDE, but XTS encryption's per-page latency causes significant performance overhead on memory-intensive workloads. Dynamically switching between CTR and XTS encryption modes and re-encrypting pages when access frequency changes incurs additional overhead that existing designs do not handle efficiently.
me: AIORE (Adaptive Incremental Offloaded Re-Encryption) combines CTR-mode encryption (low latency, parallelizable) for frequently accessed hot pages with XTS encryption (CXL IDE compliant) for cold pages. The framework dynamically selects the encryption scheme per page based on tracked access frequency using a lightweight monitoring mechanism. When a page's access pattern changes (cold-to-hot or hot-to-cold), AIORE performs incremental re-encryption, processing only the modified page rather than the entire memory region. Re-encryption is offloaded to computation resources within the CXL memory node itself, overlapping re-encryption with ongoing memory traffic to hide latency. The scheme is evaluated using gem5 full-system simulation across diverse benchmarks.
nv: Offloading incremental per-page re-encryption to CXL memory node compute, dynamically adapting between CTR and XTS encryption based on page access frequency to minimize both security overhead and re-encryption cost.

mx.other: Security overhead reduced by 62.8% on average; overhead within 3.7% vs. insecure baseline (gem5)

th: adaptive encryption for CXL memory in trusted execution environments

t: Citadel: Rethinking Memory Allocation to Safeguard Against Inter-Domain Rowhammer Exploits
pb: Rowhammer attacks exploit DRAM's physical row-adjacency to corrupt memory rows belonging to different security domains; hardware mitigations are costly, slow to adopt, and repeatedly circumvented, while software mitigations incur large performance and memory capacity overheads or provide only partial protection.
me: Citadel is a software-based memory allocator that prevents inter-domain Rowhammer by introducing flexible security domains and physically isolating them in disjoint DRAM regions—ensuring no two domains share physically adjacent rows. The allocator tracks DRAM physical row topology and partitions the address space so that domain boundaries are always separated by guard rows or page-aligned gaps. The design supports thousands of simultaneous security domains on server systems with a 7.2% average memory overhead and no measurable performance loss, without requiring hardware changes and remaining deployable on legacy, current, and future DRAM platforms.
nv: A memory allocator that prevents Rowhammer cross-domain exploits by design through physical domain isolation in disjoint DRAM row regions, achieving security without hardware modifications, performance loss, or the excessive overhead of prior software schemes.

mx.speedup: no performance loss (0% overhead)
mx.other: 7.2% average memory overhead; 4-6x lower overhead vs. recent domain isolation schemes; supports thousands of security domains

th: memory allocator for Rowhammer security via physical domain isolation

t: Supply-Chain Attacks in Machine Learning Frameworks
pb: ML frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, HuggingFace) have a larger dependency attack surface than comparable non-ML software, yet the ML community has no higher security awareness than non-ML communities, leaving ML-specific supply-chain vulnerabilities unaddressed by existing defenses.
me: Two contributions: (1) Attack demonstration - introduces ML-specific supply-chain attacks using two Python mechanisms: (a) global variable overwriting where a compromised upstream package directly mutates PyTorch/TorchVision globals (e.g., interpolation mode enums, softmax functions, model forward methods) at import time; (b) local variable overwriting using Python's inspect module and undocumented PyFrame_LocalsToFast C API to modify in-scope variables in downstream function call stacks. Three attack types demonstrated: backdoor injection via forward function hijacking, pipeline vulnerability injection via interpolation mode swap, and model weight stealing via steganographic encoding in inference outputs. (2) Security awareness analysis - LLM-assisted analysis of 549,635 GitHub issues/PRs from Top-50 ML repositories using GPT-3.5 for coarse filtering (97.8% recall) then GPT-4 for fine-grained safeguard classification (78.9% precision, 0.85 Cohen's kappa). Compared against Top-50 Linux repositories.
nv: First systematic demonstration that Python's shared memory model enables ML-specific supply-chain attacks that manipulate model behavior (not just OS security) while evading all conventional detection; LLM-assisted large-scale security awareness study across 549k GitHub issues.

mx.llm_pipeline_recall: 97.8% recall vs manual annotations (0.85 Cohen's kappa)
mx.security_pr_acceptance_pytorch: 64.20% security PR acceptance at PyTorch (lower than most ML repos)
mx.ml_vs_linux_distribution: Similar security awareness distribution between ML and Linux communities

th: ml-security

pb: Supercomputing systems face sophisticated attacks; noisy alerts and unreliable signals mask real attacks leading to data breaches

t: Implementing Network-level QoS at HPC Datacenters to Enable Distributed Scientific Workflows
pb: HPC datacenters must simultaneously handle real-time streams (sub-millisecond latency) and bulk transfers (multi-gigabit throughput), but these objectives inherently compete on shared networks, creating performance variability.

nv: First DSCP QoS deployment at HPC datacenter local network edge, providing end-to-end performance guarantees without hardware upgrades or proprietary extensions.

t: SIREN: Software Identification and Recognition in HPC Systems
pb: HPC systems rely on monitoring and analytics for efficiency and security, but lack reliable software identification methods. Job/file names unreliable (user-provided). Application-specific insights hindered by inability to identify unknown software or recognize repeated executions across runs.
me: SIREN: Process-level data collection framework using fuzzy hashing of executable contents. Detects software similarity despite version differences or different compilation approaches. Collects process metadata, environment info, executable fuzzy hashes. Deployed on LUMI (opt-in) to demonstrate effectiveness on real HPC workloads.
nv: First process-level software identification framework for HPC using fuzzy hashing; balances identification capability with privacy preservation.

me: Per-tenant virtual control planes (vCluster); VM-based container sandboxes (Azure Container Instances); policy engine (Kyverno) for automated hardening

pb: HPC systems processing sensitive genomic data need security guarantees in multi-tenant environments; TEE overhead impact on real workloads unclear
me: Evaluation of AMD SEV and SME on BWA-MEM2 genome alignment workload; comparison across SMP, SEV+SME, and SME-only configurations with varying thread counts

pb: On exascale systems like El Capitan (1M+ CPU cores, 10K+ GPUs), OS and system services cause application interference, degrading performance and scalability
me: Two-pronged strategy: (1) isolate system services from applications via cgroup/systemd tuning, (2) apply OS-level tuning to minimize application interference; distribution-independent guide provided

t: ChatEED: An agentic retrieval assistant for accelerator operators
pb: Accelerator facility operators (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory) manage critical operations via electronic logbooks (ELOGs) but face challenges: ELOG entries are time-consuming, complex, brief, incomplete, jargon-filled, and inconsistently structured. With thousands of records spanning decades, retrieving and interpreting critical information is difficult.

System designed through operator interviews and workflow analysis.

t: CASSE: Targeted Threat Modeling for Data Management Libraries

t: Secure In-Storage Execution of VTK Workloads on Modern Parallel NFS Data Servers
pb: Scientific visualization on large datasets is bottlenecked by data movement from storage servers to compute clients; moving terabytes across network for filtering wastes bandwidth and latency.
me: pNFS-based pushdown architecture offloading VTK pipeline stages (read, filter) to data servers. FUSE-based interface for client-server communication. Leverages pNFS client location awareness and Linux enhancements for efficient local storage access. Preserves user credentials and permission checks.
nv: First practical in-storage execution system for VTK on pNFS with FUSE interface; demonstrates 6–7× speedup via data filtering at source.
th: Data-parallel visualization via in-storage processing

t: SHAKTI: Securing Hardware IPs by Cascade Gated Multiplexer-Based Logic Obfuscation
pb: Logic locking vulnerable to SAT/structural learning attacks; MUX-based locking susceptible despite effectiveness
me: SHAKTI/SHAKTI+: cascade gated MUX-based locking with daisy-chained structure; 64-128 bit keys
nv: Cascade gated MUX locking resistant to SAT/SCOPE attacks with 19.32-19.45% area overhead
th: Hardware security and trust

t: A Tug-of-War Between Static and Dynamic Memory in Intel SGX
pb: Intel SGX enclaves balance static memory (allocated at enclave creation) and dynamic memory (allocated at runtime). Improper allocation strategy causes significant performance degradation due to expensive page management operations.
me: Profile-guided optimizer (Harmony) analyzing impact of dynamic memory management on application performance. Suggests near-optimal static/dynamic memory distribution based on profiling.
nv: Profile-guided optimization achieving 68% latency improvement over purely dynamic allocation and 29% improvement over purely static allocation.
th: Memory optimization for trusted execution environments

t: Codesign for Broadcast Addressing Biochip Towards Tamper-Resistance and Enhanced Reliability
pb: Digital Microfluidic Biochips (DMFB) using broadcast addressing are vulnerable to actuation sequence tampering attacks that manipulate assay results. Existing tamper-resistance solutions lack feasible wire-routing implementations. Higher electrode switching activity degrades reliability.
me: Novel pin-mapping method for broadcast addressing biochips that jointly optimizes: (1) tamper-resistance via stealthy attack detection, (2) feasible wire-routing solutions, (3) reduced switching toggles for enhanced reliability.
nv: First pin-mapping method combining tamper-resistance, wire-routing feasibility, and reliability optimization for broadcast addressing DMFBs.
th: Bioelectronic_Device_Security

t: hbcLock: Encrypted RF Communication Utilizing Body-Coupled Keys for the Internet of Bodies
pb: Wearable devices transmitting sensitive health data via RF (BLE, Wi-Fi) face eavesdropping risks. Traditional encryption key management is cumbersome and insecure for implanted or wearable bioelectronics.
me: hbcLock system combining RF encryption (BLE/Wi-Fi) with body-coupled key transfer. Wearable encrypts ECG data with key, transmits encrypted data over RF, and simultaneously transfers unencrypted key through body tissue. Receiver captures key from body contact only, then decrypts RF-received data.
nv: First demonstration of practical hybrid system combining RF communication with human-body-channel key establishment for wearable bioelectronics.
th: IoT_and_Wearable_Security

t: True-PolyTronik: Securing Circuits Against Laser Logic State Imaging Attack Using RFET
pb: Optical Probing (OP) with Laser Logic State Imaging (LLSI) attack can extract static transistor state from SRAM, combinational circuits, and sequential logic by modulating power supply at low frequency/amplitude. Existing mitigation techniques are power-hungry, require large supply modulation, or need costly laser sensors.
me: Reconfigurable Field Effect Transistor (RFET) technology for LLSI mitigation. RFETs function as programmable PMOS/NMOS via reconfiguration. Design RFET-based logic cells that: (1) detect small power supply modulation, (2) corrupt internal state upon LLSI attack via biased program pins. Biasing circuitry provides stable voltage to program pins during attack. Evaluation on combinational and D-latch cells.
nv: First RFET-based defense against LLSI attacks, exploiting runtime transistor reconfiguration for state corruption without external laser sensors or large power supply modulation.
th: Hardware_Security_and_Side_Channel_Protection

t: Serialized Control Interface ASIC for Distributed Controllers of Space-Borne RADAR
pb: SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar) payloads require distributed control hierarchy with bulky interconnect lines between central and distributed controllers, increasing complexity, size, weight, and harness complexity.
me: Integrated SCI ASIC (Serialized Control Interface) housed inside TR Module as a single IC component, replacing separate TRC subsystem. Uses pattern generator concept to generate signals internally, eliminating need for separate differential inter-connect lines for telecommand, telemetry, and radar timing.
nv: Integration of TRC functionality into single IC (SCI ASIC), elimination of bulky interconnect harness through on-chip signal generation via pattern generator.
th: Power-efficient integration and miniaturization

t: TRANSPOSE: Circuit Transformations for Power Side-Channel Security at Register Transfer Level
pb: Power side-channel attacks (PSCAs) on cryptographic hardware can leak secrets by passively probing overall device power consumption. Correlation between secret data and power consumption enables attackers to recover cryptographic keys.
me: Automated circuit transformation at RTL analyzing sensitive registers to: (1) duplicate sub-circuits influencing sensitive register outputs, (2) apply register pushing/balancing, (3) employ clock gating for obfuscation. Validates against Test Vector Leakage Assessment (TVLA).
nv: Automated RTL-level circuit transformations for PSCA hardening combining register duplication, balancing, and clock gating to randomize power consumption and reduce dynamic power.
th: Hardware security and side-channel attack mitigation

t: DuRTL - Information Flow Analysis Tool for Register Transfer Level Hardware Designs
pb: Understanding and comprehending unknown or legacy hardware designs written in Verilog/VHDL is challenging. Information flow tracking is critical for security analysis, verification, and design understanding but lacks accessible tools.
me: DuRTL implements Hardware Information Flow Tracking (IFT) using tagging mechanism. Unique tags injected into hardware designs; each tag associates a signal at a specific time with information flow during circuit traversal.
nv: Open-source C++ tool for RTL-level information flow analysis supporting Verilog and VHDL, enabling automated tracking of information propagation through unknown hardware designs.
th: Hardware design analysis and verification tools

t: RISC-V Based Secure Processor Architecture for Return Address Protection
pb: RISC-V embedded systems vulnerable to buffer overflow attacks, particularly stack-based attacks that alter program control flow. Memory-based attacks are significant challenge for RISC-V security.
me: Hardware-based approach leveraging existing Return Address Stack (RAS) with minimal microarchitecture changes and limited software overhead. Protects against buffer overflow attacks targeting control flow. Tested with buffer-intensive benchmarks and RIPE benchmark.
nv: Low-overhead RISC-V hardware return address protection using RAS with minimal area/timing overhead; protects against BFO and Spectre RAS-related attacks.
th: Hardware-based control flow integrity for RISC-V
